questions.q: Why are debug builds (e.g. compiled with -O0) typically much slower at runtime than release builds?
options: Debug builds include extra logging statements automatically
-O0 applies essentially no optimization, trading runtime performance for a straightforward line-by-line debugging experience
Debug builds always run on a single CPU core
Debug builds use a different, slower programming language subset
questions.explain: The -O0 optimization level deliberately disables most optimizations so the generated code maps closely to the source for debugging, at the cost of significant runtime performance compared to -O2 or -O3.

questions.q: What does function inlining actually do to the compiled code?
options: It moves the function to run on a separate thread
It replaces a call to the function with a direct copy of the function's body at the call site, eliminating call overhead
It converts the function into a macro at the preprocessor stage
It forces the function to always return by reference
questions.explain: Inlining substitutes the function call with the function's own instructions directly at the call site, removing the overhead of the call/return mechanism and often enabling further cross-boundary optimization.

questions.q: What is the actual, standard-mandated primary purpose of the `inline` keyword in C++?
options: It guarantees the compiler will always inline every call to that function
It mainly permits a function to be defined identically in multiple translation units without violating the one-definition rule; actual inlining is a separate compiler decision
It disables all compiler optimizations for that function
It forces the function to run at compile time
questions.explain: The inline keyword's standard-mandated effect is primarily about relaxing the one-definition rule for functions defined in headers. Whether the compiler actually inlines a given call is a separate optimization decision based on heuristics like size and call frequency.

questions.q: Why does a constexpr function like basis_points_to_decimal(1.0), called with a literal argument, cost nothing at runtime?
options: constexpr functions are always inlined regardless of size
The compiler is able to evaluate the entire expression at compile time and bake the result into the binary as a constant
constexpr functions are removed from the binary entirely and never execute
constexpr disables type checking for the function
questions.explain: constexpr requests compile-time evaluation wherever the inputs are known at compile time (such as a literal argument), so the computation happens during compilation and the result is embedded directly as a constant, with no runtime computation.

questions.q: Why might inlining a large function hurt performance rather than help it?
options: Large functions cannot be called more than once if inlined
Inlining a large function at many call sites can bloat the binary and hurt instruction-cache locality more than it saves in call overhead
Large functions automatically become constexpr when inlined
The compiler refuses to compile large inlined functions
questions.explain: Inlining duplicates the function body at every call site. For a large function called from many places, this can significantly increase code size, which can worsen instruction-cache behavior enough to outweigh the benefit of removed call overhead — which is why compilers weigh this trade-off rather than inlining everything.
